name: Costa Rica
summary: Costa Rican health law requires any body moved internationally to be embalmed and placed in an impermeable, hermetically closed coffin, with an official death certificate, a preparation (embalming) declaration, a sworn statement that the coffin holds only the deceased, and a transit permit. The receiving funeral home clears the coffin and must organise burial quickly, as burial normally takes place within 24-36 hours unless the Ministry of Health extends the deadline.
documents: Official death certificate stating the cause of death, issued by the civil registry of the place of death
Declaration by the person who prepared the body stating the method of preparation (embalming certificate), certified by the competent authority
Sworn statement that the coffin contains only the remains of the deceased
Transit permit with the name, surname and age of the deceased, issued by the authority of the place of death
Passport or ID of the deceased; apostille and official Spanish translation for any later registration of the death in Costa Rica
coffin: Executive Decree No. 1 (La Gaceta 69, 22 March 1968) requires the body to be placed in an impermeable coffin that is hermetically closed; for air transport the coffin travels in the hold of a passenger or cargo aircraft and may be fitted with a safety valve. The coffin must carry a fixed plate showing name, age, sex and final destination, and copies of the documents travel with it. Note: Costa Rica's General Cemetery Regulation (Decree 32833-S, art. 30) prohibits in-ground burial in metal coffins or other slowly decomposing materials, so a zinc-lined shipping casket may need to be replaced or placed in a vault or niche; ask the cemetery.
embalming: Required: the 1968 decree states that the body must be adequately embalmed. Costa Rica also requires an embalming certificate to send a body abroad (Decree 32833-S, art. 67).
consular: No published consular visa of the documents was found. Costa Rica is an Apostille party; to register the death of a Costa Rican abroad with the Civil Registry (TSE) the foreign death certificate must be apostilled or authenticated and translated by an official translator. Confirm with the Costa Rican consulate whether it wants to see the shipping documents before departure.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at the arrival airport (San Jose or Liberia), with the receiving funeral home collecting the coffin. Burial must take place 24-36 hours after death unless the Ministry of Health area office (Area Rectora de Salud) grants a written extension (Decree 32833-S, art. 29 as amended by Decree 42474-S); the funeral home should request this extension for a repatriated body.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the originals travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once sealed) must fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. Costa Rican rules allow the sealed coffin on a passenger or cargo aircraft; no specific rule for private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (Juan Santamaria, San Jose, or Daniel Oduber, Liberia).
private_jet_note: Coffin must be embalmed and hermetically sealed; arrange the burial-deadline extension before landing.
export: Leaving Costa Rica: international transport needs prior authorisation from the Ministry of Health area office (Area Rectora de Salud) on: a written request by a direct relative (or the embassy for a foreigner) stating destination and route; the Civil Registry death declaration form; a sworn statement that the coffin contains only the deceased; a medical stamp and a Red Cross stamp; and an embalming certificate (Decree 32833-S, art. 67). The 1968 decree requires embalming and a hermetically closed impermeable coffin. An official autopsy is carried out when a body is to be sent abroad, except for an obviously natural death of a person over 75 (FCDO). A temporary death certificate is issued first; violent or suspicious deaths involve the OIJ and a judge.
export_points: Ministry of Health (Area Rectora) authorisation required
Embalming certificate and sworn coffin-content statement
Hermetically closed impermeable coffin
Autopsy usual unless natural death over age 75

at_a_glance.death_certificate: Official certificate with cause of death
at_a_glance.laissez_passer: Transit permit from place of death
at_a_glance.consular: Apostille and official translation for registration

steps.what: Appoint a funeral home at each end and contact the Costa Rican consulate.
Obtain the death certificate with cause of death, embalming certificate and transit permit at origin.
Sign a sworn statement that the coffin holds only the deceased; seal the embalmed body in a hermetic coffin with a name plate.
Receiving funeral home asks the Ministry of Health area office for a burial-deadline extension.
Fly with document copies attached to the coffin and originals in hand.
Customs and health clearance; funeral home collects for burial or cremation.

key_points: Embalming and a hermetically closed coffin are legal requirements
Burial normally within 24-36 hours unless the Ministry of Health extends it
Metal coffins cannot be buried in the ground; check with the cemetery
Leaving Costa Rica requires an autopsy in most cases
authority: Ministry of Health (Area Rectora de Salud); Civil Registry (Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones)

name: Panama
summary: Before shipment, the Panamanian consulate in the country of death must process the documents: for an embalmed body, the original death certificate, an original health certificate, a notarised transit permit and a notarised embalming certificate, with a consular fee of USD 30 per document at the Washington consulate. A Panamanian funeral home then clears the coffin on arrival.
documents: Original death certificate
Original health certificate (certificate of no contagious disease)
Notarised transit permit
Notarised embalming certificate
Passport or ID of the deceased
Name of the receiving Panamanian funeral home
coffin: Not specified by the consulate. Panamanian funeral directors use special caskets for international transport (FCDO). Assume a hermetically sealed, airline-compliant casket and confirm with the consulate.
embalming: Embalming is expected: the consulate's list for a body (as opposed to ashes) requires a notarised embalming certificate.
consular: The Panamanian consulate processes each document (Embassy of Panama in Washington: USD 30 per document, paid by money order, originals mailed with a prepaid return envelope). Panama is an Apostille party; other consulates may ask for apostilles and a Spanish translation, so check with the consulate covering the place of death.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at Tocumen or another international airport; a Panamanian funeral home collects. Burial in a government cemetery needs permission obtained by the undertaker (FCDO). No burial deadline for embalmed repatriated bodies was found.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the originals travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once sealed) must fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. No specific Panamanian rule for private flights carrying remains was found; land at an international airport with customs and health officers (for example Tocumen or Panama Pacifico) with the consulate-processed originals.
private_jet_note: Have the consulate process all originals before take-off; they must travel with the coffin.
export: Leaving Panama: the death is registered with the Direccion Nacional del Registro Civil (Tribunal Electoral), usually by the funeral director. Shipping usually requires the local death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains; documents for foreign use are legalised via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. A post-mortem is possible for unknown, unnatural, sudden or violent deaths, and a criminal investigation can delay release. Timing depends on circumstances.
export_points: Death registered with the Registro Civil (Tribunal Electoral)
Death certificate, embalming certificate and transfer certificate
Legalisation via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Post-mortem in unnatural deaths may delay release

at_a_glance.coffin: Sealed shipping casket; confirm with consulate
at_a_glance.arrival: Panamanian funeral home collects at airport

steps.what: Appoint a funeral home at each end and contact the Panamanian consulate covering the place of death.
Obtain the death certificate, health certificate, transit permit and embalming certificate; notarise the permit and embalming certificate.
Send the originals to the consulate with the fee and a prepaid return envelope.
Seal the embalmed body in a shipping casket and fly with the processed originals.
Customs and health clearance; the Panamanian funeral home collects for burial.

key_points: Consulate processes each document (USD 30 each in Washington)
Health certificate and notarised embalming certificate needed
Coffin rules are not published; confirm with the consulate
authority: Panamanian consulate in the country of death; Ministry of Health (MINSA); Ministry of Foreign Affairs

name: Guatemala
summary: Guatemala does not publish its entry requirements for a casket; families work through a Guatemalan consulate and a licensed funeral home. Expect an apostilled death certificate, embalming certificate and transit permit. Unembalmed bodies must normally be buried within 24 hours, so embalming is essential.
documents: Death certificate from the country of death, apostilled or legalised, with Spanish translation (confirm with consulate)
Embalming certificate
Transit / burial-transit permit from the country of death
Passport or ID of the deceased
coffin: Entry rule not published. For bodies leaving Guatemala the U.S. Embassy lists a 99% hermetically sealed metal casket, and local caskets meet international shipping requirements; use an equivalent hermetically sealed casket inbound.
embalming: Entry rule not published. Guatemalan law generally requires burial within 24 hours when the body is not embalmed, with no fixed deadline when it is embalmed (U.S. Embassy), so an embalmed body is strongly advised. Embalming is required to export a body from Guatemala.
consular: Guatemalan consulates abroad coordinate repatriations of Guatemalan nationals; Guatemala is a Hague Apostille party, so the foreign death certificate should be apostilled and translated into Spanish. Confirm with the consulate.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at La Aurora International Airport; a local funeral home collects. Burial within 24 hours applies to unembalmed bodies; embalmed bodies have no fixed deadline (U.S. Embassy).
private_aviation: No official rule for private or charter flights carrying human remains was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health officers, and confirm clearance with the local funeral home and airport authority before departure.
private_jet_note: Entry rules unpublished: confirm health and customs clearance with the consulate before take-off.
export: Leaving Guatemala: embalming is required to export a body. Documents: embalming certificate, death certificate from RENAP and a Guatemalan transit permit; the body travels in a 99% hermetically sealed metal casket, with a shipping container for air. Export follows authorisation from the sanitary authority of the Ministry of Health (MSPAS). For ashes: transit permit, cremation certificate and RENAP death certificate. Autopsy by INACIF in violent or unnatural deaths; cremation then needs a court order, which can take 8 weeks or more (U.S. Embassy). Cemetery and body-handling rules are set by Government Decree 215-2021.
export_points: Embalming, RENAP death certificate and Guatemalan transit permit
99% hermetically sealed metal casket
Ministry of Health sanitary authorisation before export
INACIF autopsy in violent deaths can delay release

at_a_glance.coffin: Hermetically sealed casket; entry rule unpublished
at_a_glance.laissez_passer: Origin transit permit; Strasbourg not applicable

steps.what: Contact the consulate of Guatemala in the country of death and appoint a funeral home at each end.
Obtain death certificate, embalming certificate and transit permit at origin; apostille the death certificate.
Consulate reviews documents and confirms entry requirements; body sealed in an air-transport casket.
Casket flown to an international airport of entry with the original documents.
Customs and health clearance; receiving funeral home collects the casket for burial.

key_points: Official entry requirements are not published; confirm with the consulate
Unembalmed bodies must be buried within 24 hours
Exports need a hermetically sealed metal casket
authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (consular affairs) and Ministry of Public Health (MSPAS); INACIF and Ministerio Publico for violent deaths

name: Honduras
summary: The Honduran consulate in the country of death issues a free Certificate of Exit of Mortal Remains (Certificado de salida de restos mortales), needed to transport the coffin or ashes to Honduras, on an apostilled death certificate, a medical certificate if death occurred in hospital, and an embalming (or cremation) certificate. A Honduran funeral home then clears the coffin on arrival.
documents: Apostilled death certificate
Medical certificate, if the death occurred in a hospital
Embalming certificate (or cremation certificate for ashes)
Certificado de salida de restos mortales issued by the Honduran consulate (requested last, once the other documents are ready)
Transit permit from the country of death and passport or ID of the deceased
coffin: Not specified by the consulate; local funeral directors use special caskets for international carriage (FCDO). Assume a hermetically sealed, airline-compliant casket.
embalming: An embalming certificate is required for the consular exit certificate for a body; cremation certificate for ashes.
consular: The Honduran consulate issues the Certificado de salida de restos mortales free of charge; at the Madrid consulate it is requested by email or in person without an appointment. The consulate does not register the death: a relative registers it with the RNP in Tegucigalpa using the apostilled death certificate. State-funded repatriation is possible only for families without resources, requested in person by a first- or second-degree relative, and only if the family has not already signed with a funeral home; it takes about 4-6 weeks.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at the international airport of entry; a local funeral home collects. Local custom is burial within 24 hours (FCDO).
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the originals travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once sealed) must fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. No specific Honduran rule for private flights carrying remains was found; land at an international airport with customs and health officers with the consular exit certificate and originals.
private_jet_note: Carry the consulate's exit certificate with the coffin; confirm airport clearance with the funeral home.
export: Leaving Honduras: a local funeral director arranges the local death certificate (in Spanish), a certificate of embalming and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains, and supplies the special casket. In violent or suspicious deaths the National Civil Police involve the Ministerio Publico and an autopsy is required. Cold storage exists in Tegucigalpa and La Ceiba but is rare elsewhere. Otherwise release usually within a few days.
export_points: Death certificate, embalming certificate and transfer permit via the funeral director
Autopsy and Ministerio Publico in violent or suspicious deaths
Cold storage mainly in Tegucigalpa and La Ceiba
Release usually within a few days if not suspicious

at_a_glance.permit: Transit permit from country of death

steps.what: Contact the Honduran consulate; decide on private or state-assisted repatriation before signing with a funeral home.
Obtain and apostille the death certificate; get the medical and embalming certificates and transit permit.
Request the free Certificado de salida de restos mortales from the consulate.
Seal the embalmed body in a shipping casket and fly with all originals.
Customs and health clearance; Honduran funeral home collects for burial.

key_points: Consular exit certificate is free and required
Do not sign with a funeral home if you need state aid
Local custom is burial within 24 hours
authority: Honduran consulate (Secretaria de Relaciones Exteriores, SRECI); Secretariat of Health; Registro Nacional de las Personas (RNP)

name: El Salvador
summary: El Salvador's Ministry of Foreign Affairs coordinates repatriations through its embassies and consulates and notifies the Ministry of Health, which sets the conditions for human remains entering the country; the detailed entry document list is not published. Expect an apostilled death certificate, embalming certificate and transit permit, and contact the Salvadoran consulate first.
documents: Death certificate from the country of death, apostilled or legalised, with Spanish translation (confirm with consulate)
Embalming certificate
Transit / burial-transit permit from the country of death
Passport or ID of the deceased
coffin: Entry rule not published. Local funeral homes use caskets and hermetically sealed containers that meet international transport requirements (U.S. Embassy); use an equivalent sealed casket inbound.
embalming: Entry rule not published. In El Salvador embalmed remains may be kept up to 30 days before burial and unembalmed remains only 48 hours (U.S. Embassy), so embalming is strongly advised for a repatriated body.
consular: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Direccion de Diaspora y Movilidad Humana) and its embassies and consulates assist with repatriation: the family applies by phone or in person, is interviewed, and provides a copy of the deceased's birth certificate and identity document; the consulate claims the remains from foreign authorities and the ministry shares the arrival itinerary and notifies the Ministry of Health. Contacts: +503 2231-1373 / 2231-2950; toll-free 1-888-301-1130 from the US and Canada; WhatsApp +503 7070-1071. El Salvador is an Apostille party; apostille and Spanish translation expected.
arrival: The Ministry of Health is notified of the arrival and sets the conditions for the entry of the remains, including special protocols where relevant. Customs and health clearance at El Salvador International Airport; a local funeral home collects. Burial within 30 days if embalmed, 48 hours if not (U.S. Embassy).
private_aviation: No official rule for private or charter flights carrying human remains was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health officers, and confirm clearance with the local funeral home and airport authority before departure.
private_jet_note: Entry rules unpublished: confirm health and customs clearance with the consulate before take-off.
export: Leaving El Salvador: the funeral home completes documentation with the Instituto de Medicina Legal, the prosecutor's office, the Civil Registry, the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the airline. Documents include the medical certificate of death, Civil Registry death certificate, export permit from the Ministry of Health and an affidavit of preparation; embalming is required for shipment to the US, with hermetically sealed containers. Autopsy is mandatory for accidental, sudden, violent or suspicious deaths and reports can take months. Unclaimed remains may be buried in a common grave after about one week (U.S. Embassy).
export_points: Ministry of Health export permit and Civil Registry death certificate
Embalming and hermetically sealed container for shipment
Mandatory autopsy for sudden, violent or suspicious deaths
Unclaimed remains may be buried after about one week

at_a_glance.laissez_passer: Origin transit permit; Strasbourg not applicable
at_a_glance.permit: Ministry of Health sets entry conditions

steps.what: Call the Salvadoran consulate or Foreign Ministry and appoint a funeral home at each end.
Provide the deceased's birth certificate and ID copy; obtain death certificate, embalming certificate and transit permit at origin.
Consulate checks documents and confirms entry; body embalmed and sealed in a shipping casket.
Foreign Ministry receives the itinerary and notifies the Ministry of Health.
Health and customs clearance; funeral home collects for burial.

key_points: The Ministry of Health sets the conditions for remains entering the country
Foreign Ministry hotline 1-888-301-1130 from the US and Canada
Embalmed bodies may be kept 30 days, unembalmed only 48 hours
authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Direccion de Diaspora y Movilidad Humana) and Ministry of Health (MINSAL); Instituto de Medicina Legal

name: Nicaragua
summary: Nicaragua does not publish an entry procedure for a casket online. A 1968 decree adopted the Pan American Health Organization norms on international transport of bodies (official cause-of-death certificate, preparation declaration, transit permit, impermeable sealed coffin), but its current application could not be confirmed; confirm with a Nicaraguan consulate and a licensed funeral home.
documents: Official certificate of cause of death from the civil registry of the place of death (apostilled, with Spanish translation; confirm with consulate)
Declaration by the person who prepared the body stating the method used and that the coffin contains only the deceased (embalming certificate)
Transit permit with name, surname and age of the deceased, issued by the authority of the place of death
Passport or ID of the deceased
coffin: Executive Decree No. 12 of 1968 (La Gaceta No. 100, 7 May 1968) adopted PAHO Resolution XXIX: the body travels in an impermeable coffin sealed hermetically (metal lining soldered, or plastic or rubber seals), or in a heat-sealed plastic receptacle inside an ordinary coffin; the coffin carries a fixed plate with name, age, sex and destination. Text consulted in a legal database, not on an official portal; current enforcement not verified.
embalming: Under the 1968 PAHO norms the body is either disinfected and wrapped, or embalmed (arterial and cavity); embalming is mandatory if death was from a quarantinable disease. Locally, bodies are not usually embalmed but embalming is done on request for repatriation (FCDO).
consular: Nicaraguan consulates are the point of contact. Nicaragua is a Hague Apostille party; apostille and Spanish translation expected. Confirm with the consulate.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at Managua international airport; a local funeral home collects. Burial deadline not officially published.
private_aviation: No official rule for private or charter flights carrying human remains was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health officers, and confirm clearance with the local funeral home and airport authority before departure.
private_jet_note: Entry rules unpublished: confirm health and customs clearance with the consulate before take-off.
export: Leaving Nicaragua: authorisation from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Health is needed for repatriation (British Embassy). The hospital medical report (epicrisis) must be registered at the Registro Civil of the municipality; it is issued about two days after request. Autopsies only when a crime or accident is presumed (Instituto de Medicina Legal). Embalming on request for repatriation. All documents are in Spanish.
export_points: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health authorisation required
Death registered at the municipal Registro Civil (about 2 days)
Embalming on request for repatriation
Autopsy by Instituto de Medicina Legal if crime or accident presumed

Casket flown to an international airport of entry with the original documents.

1968 decree follows PAHO norms: sealed impermeable coffin and transit permit
Exit needs both Foreign Affairs and Health ministry authorisation

name: Belize
summary: Belize does not publish official entry requirements for a casket online, and no import provision was found in the Public Health Act; confirm with the Belize consulate or embassy and a licensed funeral home. Expect a death certificate, embalming certificate and transit permit (English-language documents accepted).
documents: Death certificate from the country of death (apostilled; English is an official language of Belize)
Embalming certificate
Transit / burial-transit permit from the country of death
Passport or ID of the deceased
coffin: No official published entry rule found; assume a sealed, airline-compliant casket.
embalming: Not officially published for entry; embalming is standard for international shipment.
consular: Belize consulates and embassies are the point of contact. Belize is a Hague Apostille party; no translation needed for English documents.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at Philip S. W. Goldson International Airport; a local funeral home collects. Burial deadline not officially published. Cremation in Belize needs the permission of the Director of Health Services (Public Health Act).
private_aviation: No official rule for private or charter flights carrying human remains was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health officers, and confirm clearance with the local funeral home and airport authority before departure.
private_jet_note: Entry rules unpublished: confirm health and customs clearance with the consulate before take-off.
export: Leaving Belize: local undertakers register the death with the Vital Statistics Unit and arrange a Belize death certificate to accompany the remains. A post-mortem is normally performed in all cases and always when death is not natural; a Coroner (usually a magistrate) investigates unnatural deaths. Personal belongings cannot be shipped with the body. Mortuaries are at regional hospitals; standards vary.
export_points: Death registered by the undertaker with the Vital Statistics Unit
Post-mortem normally performed in all cases
Coroner involved for unnatural deaths
Personal belongings cannot travel with the body

at_a_glance.embalming: Standard for shipment; entry rule unpublished
at_a_glance.laissez_passer: Origin transit permit; Strasbourg not applicable

steps.what: Contact the consulate of Belize in the country of death and appoint a funeral home at each end.
Obtain death certificate, embalming certificate and transit permit at origin; apostille the death certificate.
Consulate reviews documents and confirms entry requirements; body sealed in an air-transport casket.
Casket flown to an international airport of entry with the original documents.
Customs and health clearance; receiving funeral home collects the casket for burial.

Cremation needs permission from the Director of Health Services
Autopsy is normal in Belize, which can delay outgoing repatriation

name: Dominican Republic
summary: The Dominican consulate in the country of death processes the shipping documents: for a body, the original death certificate from the vital records office, a certificate of no contagious disease from the local health department, and a notarised embalming certificate signed by the funeral director or embalmer. The receiving Dominican funeral home clears the coffin at the airport.
documents: Original death certificate issued by the vital records office of the place of death
Certificate of no contagious disease (certificacion de no contagio) from the local health department
Embalming certificate signed by the funeral director or embalmer, notarised
Removal or transit permit from the country of departure
Passport or identity document of the deceased and name of the receiving Dominican funeral home
coffin: Not specified on the consulate page. A hermetically sealed coffin is the usual international standard for air transport; confirm with the Dominican consulate and the airline.
embalming: Required in practice: the consulate's list for a body includes a notarised embalming certificate. The UK government also lists an embalming certificate among documents for repatriation out of the Dominican Republic.
consular: Documents are submitted to the Dominican consulate covering the place of death (the New York consulate publishes the checklist; tel. +1 212 768 2480, infony@mirex.gob.do). For cremated remains the death and cremation certificates must be apostilled by the US Department of State. Holders of a valid Dominican electronic ordinary passport are covered by a free repatriation insurance with Seguros Reservas (up to USD 9,000; notify within 48 hours of the death; 6-month waiting period for death from illness), per the Direccion General de Pasaportes. Dominican consulates also sell a repatriation plan (e.g. Madrid).
arrival: Not published officially. The receiving Dominican funeral home normally handles customs and health clearance at the airport. Confirm burial or cremation formalities with the funeral home.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (for example Santo Domingo Las Americas or Punta Cana) and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
private_jet_note: Have the consulate process the originals before take-off; they travel with the coffin.
export: To send a body out of the Dominican Republic, the death is registered at the local Civil Registry office (Oficialia del Registro Civil), usually within about 3 working days. All foreign nationals who die in the country undergo a post-mortem at the Pathology Institute in Santo Domingo or Santiago. The UK government lists the documents for repatriation as the civil registry death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Dominican death certificates are in Spanish and do not state the cause of death, which matters for destinations (such as the US) that require it unless the body is embalmed.
export_points: Death registered at the local Civil Registry, about 3 working days
Post-mortem for all foreign nationals at the Pathology Institute
Embalming certificate and permission to transfer the remains needed
Death certificate in Spanish without cause of death

at_a_glance.coffin: Sealed coffin usual; not officially specified

Dominican e-passport holders have repatriation insurance up to USD 9,000
Foreigners dying in the country always have a post-mortem
authority: Dominican consulate in the country of departure (Ministry of Foreign Affairs, MIREX); Civil Registry and Pathology Institute (exit)
